title: Sa'di of Shiraz
hookLine: the poet of Shiraz, whose lines say that humans are limbs of one body

cards: A stubbed toe. That's all it takes. One small toe meets the leg of a table, and suddenly the whole of you is involved.
Your hands grab your foot. Your face twists. Your voice says something you'd rather your grandmother hadn't heard.
Nobody in your body says, that's the toe's problem. A poet from Shiraz took that ordinary fact and turned it into a Persian poem about every human being on earth. Today: Sa'di of Shiraz.

teach.h: THE ORCHARD AND THE ROSE GARDEN.
teach.b: Sa'di is remembered for two books: the Bustan, the orchard, in verse, and the Gulistan, the rose garden, in prose with poems woven through.
The Gulistan is full of short stories about kings and beggars, judges and dervishes, travelers and fools, each ending with a lesson that often stings a little.

teach.h: A TRAVELER WHO WAS ONCE A PRISONER.
teach.b: Sa'di was a traveler himself. In one of his own stories, he is taken prisoner far from home and put to work digging a trench, until an acquaintance pays to set him free. He knew what it was to be a stranger.
In the Gulistan comes the poem, here in paraphrase.

teach.h: THE CHILDREN OF ADAM ARE LIMBS.
teach.b: The children of Adam are limbs of one another, made from one essence. When the world gives pain to one limb, the other limbs cannot rest.
And if you feel nothing at the suffering of others, you do not deserve to be called human. The picture was not new.

A saying of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari, describes believers in their mercy and love for one another as one body: when one part aches, the whole body answers with sleeplessness and fever.
Sa'di's poem, many readers note, widens that body to all the children of Adam. Not only my family. Not only my faith.
Anyone made of the same clay. A poem about strangers, written by a man who had been one, and built on a body that can't ignore its own toe.

how: Sa'di's Gulistan is a classic of Persian schooling, and his lines on the children of Adam are memorized and quoted across Iran and the Persian-speaking world.

games.q: you're Sa'di. you have the Prophet's saying about believers as one body. you're writing for everyone who will read the rose garden. how wide do you draw the body?
games.why: he writes that the children of Adam are limbs of one another, and that whoever feels nothing at others' pain does not deserve to be called human.

practice: Notice your own body for a moment, feet, hands, chest, all of it answering to all of it.

Then picture one stranger you'll likely pass today, the person at the register or a neighbor whose name you don't know, and see them as a limb of the same body you belong to. If you pray, ask for their good; if not, simply wish it.
